Abstract

Evolutionary rescue refers to the process by which a population that is declining towards extinction due to an environmental stressor adapts to said stressor, recovering in population size. Previous models of evolutionary rescue have typically modelled density-dependence using simple logistic growth-type models, assuming that an environmental change either affects the intrinsic growth rates or carrying capacity of a population. Here, we analyze evolutionary rescue in a mechanistic consumer-resource model, modelling density-dependence explicitly through consumption of a finite resource. Here we submit data from forward-time, individual-based simulations in which we explore how the life-history (low fecundity & high survivorship vs. high fecundity & low survivorship) and genetic architecture (one-locus model, polygenic model) of a consumer population interacts with the ecological effects of an environmental change (whether it influences resource acquisition rates, conversion efficiencies, or mortality). We find that evolutionary rescue is indeed highly dependent on the affected ecological trait and interacts with the resident life-history of the population.
